chief_complaint: bruises on arms and back with missed follow-ups and weight loss
hpi_details: 78-year-old female with a history of a stroke one year ago (resulting in mild right weakness but intact cognition) is brought to the clinic by her son. The son attempts to answer all questions for her and dominates the interview. The patient presents with a history of missed follow-up appointments, noticeable weight loss, and unexplained bruises on both upper arms (resembling grip marks) and her back. When successfully interviewed alone, she discloses that her son controls her pension card and shoves her when he is angry. She admits to being afraid of him but explicitly states she does not want him to be punished.
ideas: believes her son is just stressed from caring for her and does not mean to cause real harm
concerns: fears that if the doctor reports this, her son will be sent to jail and she will be left completely alone
expectations: hopes the doctor will treat her back pain and injuries without involving the police or punishing her son
pmh: Stroke one year ago with residual mild right-sided weakness. Intact cognition.
social_hx: Widowed. Lives with her son who is her primary caregiver and manages all her finances.

boundaries_and_exceptions: While a patient's capacity and autonomy must generally be respected, mandatory reporting laws for elder abuse supersede patient confidentiality.
If the patient lacked decision-making capacity, adult protective services would take a more directive role in placement, though here the patient has intact cognition.
common_misconceptions: Assuming bruises in the elderly are always due to falls or age-related capillary fragility without considering non-accidental trauma.
Allowing a dominant caregiver to remain in the room for the entire interview without making an excuse to speak to the patient alone.
Believing that mandatory reporting can be bypassed if the patient has intact cognition and explicitly requests not to involve authorities.
Failing to recognize financial exploitation (e.g., caregiver withholding pension cards) as a form of abuse.
core_concepts: Elder abuse encompasses physical, emotional, sexual, and financial exploitation, as well as neglect, often perpetrated by a family caregiver.
A critical step in evaluation is interviewing the patient alone to ensure safety, assess capacity, and provide a secure environment for disclosure.
Detailed documentation of injuries, including their shape (e.g., grip marks) and location, is medico-legally required.
In South Korea, healthcare providers are mandatory reporters of suspected elder abuse to the elder protection agency or police, regardless of the patient's reluctance.
Management involves a multidisciplinary approach including social work, ensuring immediate safety, and respecting the patient's autonomy to the extent safely and legally possible while intervening.
dangerous_errors: Discharging the patient back to an unsafe home environment without a safety assessment or social work involvement.
Confronting the suspected abuser directly, which may escalate violence against the patient.
Failing to fulfill mandatory reporting requirements, leading to continued or escalating abuse.
Overlooking potential hidden injuries, such as osteoporotic fractures from being shoved, by failing to order appropriate imaging.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: bruises on arms and back with missed follow-ups and weight loss.
Key HPI features: Son dominating the interview and answering for the patient. Patient disclosure (when alone) that her son shoves her when angry and controls her pension card.
Objective/Exam findings: Bruises on bilateral upper arms suggestive of grip marks, and bruising on the back. Frail appearance with weight loss.
Relevant background/PMH: Mild right-sided weakness from previous stroke making her physically dependent on the caregiver.
management_principles: Interview the patient alone: use a pretext such as the physical exam or taking vitals to separate the patient from the caregiver.
Assess immediate safety and determine if the patient can safely return home; involve hospital social work immediately.
Perform a complete physical examination to document all injuries meticulously.
Order a spine X-ray to evaluate for osteoporotic fractures given the back pain and history of being shoved.
Report to the local elder protection agency, as clinicians are mandatory reporters for elder abuse.

reference_soap.assessment: 1. Suspected elder abuse (physical abuse and financial exploitation) by primary caregiver. 2. Back pain with suspected osteoporotic vertebral fracture secondary to trauma. 3. Unintentional weight loss, likely related to neglect or financial abuse.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 82, BP 138/85, Temp 36.8C. Weight: 48 kg (down 4 kg from last visit). General: frail, appears anxious. Neuro: intact cognition, mild right-sided weakness (known). Skin: multiple ecchymoses on bilateral upper arms (resembling grip marks) in varying stages of healing. Large bruise on the mid-back with localized tenderness over the thoracic spine.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Immediate safety assessment: consult medical social worker to evaluate safe discharge versus admission. 2. Mandatory reporting: notify the local elder protection agency as legally required. 3. Diagnostics: obtain Thoracic/Lumbar spine X-rays to rule out vertebral compression fracture. 4. Documentation: photograph and meticulously document all injuries in the medical record. 5. Support: reassure patient, provide emotional support, and explain the reporting process gently.
reference_soap.subjective: 78F with a history of stroke presents with missed follow-ups, weight loss, and bruising. Brought by her son who dominates the conversation and answers for her. When interviewed alone, the patient reveals her son controls her pension card and shoves her when he is angry, causing the bruises. She expresses fear but begs that he not be punished, as he is her only family.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical 'red flags' of elder abuse, including unexplained bruising in unusual locations, weight loss, missed appointments, and an overly dominant caregiver.
Demonstrate the essential communication skill of successfully separating a patient from a suspected abusive caregiver to conduct a private interview.
Apply local mandatory reporting laws for elder abuse while maintaining a supportive and empathetic therapeutic alliance with the victim.
Formulate a safe management plan that addresses immediate physical needs (e.g., imaging for trauma) and social safety (e.g., social work consultation).

teaching.diagnosis: Elder abuse (physical abuse and financial exploitation)
differentials: Accidental falls due to post-stroke weakness

must_ask.say: I need to do a physical exam now, so I will ask your son to step out into the waiting room for a few minutes.
Now that we are alone, can you tell me exactly how you got these bruises on your arms and back?
Have you had any recent falls or trouble walking since your stroke?
Do you feel safe at home, or are you ever afraid of your son?
Who manages your money and pension card?
I understand you do not want him punished, but my first priority is keeping you safe and I am legally required to report this.

teaching.one_liner: An elderly stroke survivor presenting with suspicious grip-mark bruises, missed appointments, and a dominant son controlling her finances requires separation for a private interview and mandatory reporting for elder abuse.
red_flags: Bruises on bilateral upper arms resembling grip marks
Son answering all questions and refusing to leave the patient's side initially
Caregiver withholding financial resources such as a pension card

history.answer: My back has been hurting terribly, and I've noticed all these dark bruises showing up on my arms and back.
Thank you, doctor. It is a relief to speak privately, but please don't tell my son that I talked to you.
A few days ago at home, my son got very upset when I couldn't move fast enough, and he grabbed me tightly and shoved me into the hallway wall.
He gripped both of my arms so hard it left finger-shaped marks, and when he pushed me, my mid-back slammed into the wall corner, which still aches badly.
No, he has never choked me, hit my head, or made me pass out, and I haven't had any dizziness or trouble swallowing.
It didn't use to be like this, but over the past few months it has been happening more often whenever he gets stressed, though he has never threatened me with weapons or threatened to kill me.
I am scared to go home when he is angry, but right now he is waiting outside in the waiting room and I don't have anywhere else to sleep.
No, it is just the two of us living together in the apartment; there are no young children or other relatives.
He took my bank book and pension card months ago and keeps all the money, so I cannot buy food or get my prescriptions unless he chooses to buy them.
He gets annoyed if I try to call my old church friends, so I have mostly stopped talking to anyone outside our home.
No, heaven forbid, nothing sexual has ever happened.
I lost about four kilograms because there isn't always enough groceries at home, and we missed my appointments because he refused to bring me when he was busy.
I have not tripped or fallen recently; my right side is still a bit weak from my stroke last year, but I walk carefully inside the house.
I have terrible trouble falling asleep, and whenever I hear heavy footsteps or a door slam, my heart starts pounding with terror.
No, I have never wanted to harm myself or end my life; I just want peace at home.
I don't have any close relatives left since my husband died, and I have never reached out to welfare centers or reported him to the police before.
I just want medical care for my aching back and bruises, but please do not call the police or punish my son.
I think he is just exhausted and overwhelmed from taking care of a sick mother; he does not truly mean to be cruel.
I am terrified that if you report this, the police will lock him up in prison, and I will be left completely alone with no one to look after me.
I am hoping you can check my spine, give me some pain medication, and keep this between us.
I had an ischemic stroke one year ago, which left me with mild weakness in my right arm and leg, but my mind is still clear.
I was admitted to the hospital for two weeks when I had the stroke a year ago for treatment and rehabilitation, but I've had no other surgeries.
I take aspirin, atorvastatin, and amlodipine every morning, though I sometimes run out when my son forgets to pick up refills.
No, I have no known allergies to any medicines.
I have never smoked a cigarette in my life.
I do not drink any alcohol.
I am a retired homemaker and widow; I rely entirely on my son for cooking, chores, and managing our daily life.
Both of my parents passed away of natural old age, and there is no family history of bleeding disorders or bone disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 138/85 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Frail, visibly underweight elderly woman appearing anxious, guarded, and distressed.
Alert and fully oriented to time, place, and person with coherent speech and intact cognition.
No facial bruising, periorbital ecchymosis, or subconjunctival hemorrhage; pupils equal and reactive.
Multiple ecchymoses on bilateral upper arms resembling thumb and fingertip grip marks in varying stages of healing; no burns, cuts, or petechiae on the neck.
Large resolving bruise across the mid-back with marked localized point tenderness over the mid-thoracic spinous processes; straight-leg raise is negative bilaterally.
No rib cage deformity, chest wall tenderness, or crepitus on palpation.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended without guarding or palpable masses.
Mild right-sided weakness with motor strength 4/5 in the right upper and lower extremities; 5/5 strength on the left.
Slow, mildly asymmetric gait with right-sided dragging, requiring supervision, but without cerebellar ataxia.
